articles.title: Next-generation airlift study stuck in limbo, awaiting FY-27 budget
articles.description: KISSIMMEE, FL -- Air Mobility Command cannot begin its long-awaited analysis of alternatives for the Next Generation Airlift program until the fiscal year 2027 budget is approved, putting the effort's ambitious six-month timeline on hold. “Next Generation Airlift (NGAL) is a new start, and we would expect a delay under a continuing resolution,” an AMC spokesperson told Inside Defense. “The NGAL AOA could begin once Congress provides the necessary funding and authority, either through an appropriations act or through a provision in a continuing resolution that permits the work to start.” The government is currently operating under a continuing resolution that expires Dec. 11, limiting spending to FY-26 levels and preventing new programs from kicking off. Lawmakers are now sorting through a lame-duck agenda, but the prospect of passing next year's defense budget in the coming weeks is becoming increasingly slim with Republicans set to lose control of both chambers in January. Without any specific waiver in an extended or second continuing resolution to initiate the NGAL AOA, the program may fall short of its schedule goals. AMC wants to pursue an accelerated AOA that spans six months rather than the traditional 18- to 20-month timeframe, leaders previously stated. The service is asking for about $8.9 million in FY-27 to begin the AOA and other NGAL concept-refinement activities, according to FY-27 budget request documents. The Air Force is aiming to field NGAL initially in 2038. The future strategic airlifter should be a single capability able to fly farther and carry more compared to the C-17A Globemaster III -- which is set to fly through 2075 -- and C-5M Super Galaxy -- expected to retire by 2045 -- according to a request for information issued in June. NGAL’s capability attributes are expected to be sorted out during the AOA process, leaders said during the Airlift/Tanker Association’s annual conference last week, noting all options are on the table. “We're not just talking about platforms here, right? Strategic airlift is not just a flight; it's a cycle,” Col. Derrick McClain, AMC deputy director of strategy, plans, requirements and programs, said during a panel discussion here. “You’ve got to take off after you unload the cargo. You've got to fly to your destination, land, offload, onload -- potentially under threat,” he said. “And if the flight time is less than the ground time, that's a missed opportunity.” The upcoming NGAL AOA will assess constraints to onload and offload times, according to McClain, and consider a range of solutions from a new design to the modification of an existing platform. The Air Force is weighing reopening Boeing’s C-17 production line, which has been closed since 2015, as part of its analysis. “I think [NGAL] needs to be something that is as dependable or more so than the C-17, and that's a tall order, right? So looking at the C-17 is one of the options on the table, but there's tons of other things,” AMC commander Lt. Gen. Daniel Tulley said during a separate panel. But it may not be as easy a solution as it sounds: restarting C-17 production could prove to be too expensive a feat to get any support, a congressional aide told Inside Defense on the sidelines of the conference on the condition of anonymity. There are also concerns with the C-17 engine. One airman during the panel asked McClain how viable restarting the line could be since the program has an extremely limited number of spares. The airman described instances in which maintainers had to cannibalize engine components to complete repairs. “As we go into the analysis of alternatives for NGAL, we're absolutely going to be looking at what kind of engines are required to set the enterprise,” McClain said during a question-and-answer session. “In that space of the mid-class thrust engine, there are less options than small and large class, and so we're talking about that.” Other possible NGAL ideas include a blended-wing body style airlifter, Tulley said, or an aircraft which requires only a single pilot and uses some artificial intelligence to assist with some basic tasks in the cockpit. “There are a number of characteristics and attributes that we want in that next-gen airlifter. We're putting that together as we go through the AOA,” Tulley said. “But I don't know exactly what it looks like yet. We're looking at all options and anything, any good ideas, we're happy to take them in.” Autonomy is on the table, too, service Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach told an audience of airmen during his keynote address. He described a possible future scenario in which a fleet of cargo drones moved parts, fuel, weapons and even people around contested environments. The idea is to avoid burning an entire C-17 sortie by instead sending an autonomous airlifter with the necessary equipment, such as a retrofitted part, to the right location in a shorter amount of time. The crew on site could then take the new part to fix a jet there and put the old part back into the drone to be sent to the depot. “I think it would be a much more effective way of making sure the parts are moving at the pace and the scale that we need to,” Wilsbach said.
